paras: The lynching of Aldy Neal was the hanging of a man accused of horse theft by about twenty armed, masked men near Rockford, Spokane County, Washington Territory, in May 1882. Neal was taken from the citizens conveying him to Cheney and hanged from a tree, and the lynchers were not identified. A wire dispatch carried the news nationally, and several western papers condemned the killing as murder.

According to a Walla Walla dispatch, the Neal family had lived at Rockford and was known as "a tough set," and one son had been indicted for creating a disturbance at a Methodist church. Most of the family moved to Montana, while Aldy and a sister remained; in November he was arrested for stealing a horse but left the country and joined the family. Other reports said he had been captured the previous fall with seventy-five stolen horses and escaped, and the earliest said he was caught running stolen horses to Montana.

On a Sunday in May, Neal returned to Rockford, saying he had come for his sister, and a party of citizens who knew he was wanted by Sheriff Hatten surrounded the house and captured him. After threats of lynching, a detail of citizens set out at daylight Monday to take him to Cheney, with Neal strapped to a saddle. In a thick growth of timber about twenty heavily armed men with the lower parts of their faces masked stopped the guard at gunpoint.

Two men unstrapped Neal and led him into the timber, where he begged for his life and promised to confess and leave forever. His captors told him his time had come, threw a rope over a limb and hanged him, then rode off. His body was found hanging from a tree by the roadside.

The men who had arrested Neal said they could not identify any of the lynchers. According to the Standard, the lynchers then went in search of William McCane, who had escaped from the Cheney jail in April. No report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The first notice came in a Spokane Falls special to the Lewiston Teller dated May 23, which called the victim "Alday Newell" and a horse thief. A San Francisco wire from Walla Walla, headlined "LYNCHED," described "Andy Neal" as "a horse thief, and generally disreputable character" hanged by "the vigilants"; the brief ran from Dallas and St. Paul to Wilmington.

The Sacramento Record-Union, which printed the full Walla Walla account, followed with an editorial, "A Barbarous Mob Murder," arguing that no specific crime seemed to have been charged and that every lyncher "deserves the fate which they inflicted upon their helpless victim." The Corvallis Gazette headlined its item "Murder by Lynchlag," the Washington Standard called the act "entirely unwarranted," and the Walla Walla Union, quoted in Idaho, called it among history's most "shocking and barberous scenes."

Montana papers were more mixed: the Butte Miner and the River Press repeated the Walla Walla Statesman's description of Neal as a "bad man" from Montana, though the River Press added that the lynching was "considered an outrage." The Benton Weekly Record reprinted the Statesman's account in July under the headline "Died With His Boots On," calling the hanging a "necktie festival." No paper described the episode in racial terms.

Accounts differed on the date: the Walla Walla reports placed the hanging after daylight on Monday, the Teller and the Standard on Sunday night, the Omaha Bee on "the 21st," and the Vancouver Independent on "May 28th," a date later than the first reports. The Standard's version, reprinted in Astoria and Vancouver, placed the event at "Rockport," thirty-five miles east of Cheney, and said Neal surrendered on a promise of trial to Starr, Henderson and Gilbert, with shots exchanged before he was given up. The Walla Walla account said instead that the guard was stopped "without a word being said," a mile and a half or half a mile from Rockford, and the Washington Standard placed the lynching in the Cœur d'Alene valley.
The custodians were a detail of citizens in the Walla Walla account but "the Sheriff" in the Corvallis Gazette and "the officers" in the Washington Standard.

Neal was hanged by about twenty men who took him from the citizens conveying him to Cheney, without any legal process, after he had been accused of horse theft (A3, A20, A27). No paper names his race or the lynchers' race (A3, A16).

Independent accounts from a Spokane Falls special (A1), a Walla Walla dispatch and the Walla Walla Statesman (A3, A27), and 'the Standard' (A16) agree that he was seized near Rockford, taken from a guard and hanged.
